source.title: Layer-wise Regularized Dropout for Neural Language Models
source.authors: Shi-Wen Ni; Min Yang; Rui-Feng Xu; Cheng-Ming Li; Xi-Ping Hu

record.tranche_reason: The paper builds LR-Drop on dropout and evaluates its own regularization method; it does not test the listed claim versions about memorization, architecture, optimizers, batch size, ordinary dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.gate_note: The GLUE, translation, summarization, ablation, training-set-size, and dropout-count results evaluate LR-Drop or its components. They do not isolate the effect named by a claim version, so they are not catalog rows. The loss-landscape analysis is a reported measurement relevant to the claim's subject but does not measure train-test gap or magnitude-aware sharpness.
record.test_reason: LR-Drop uses dropout to construct sub-models and evaluates added consistency regularization. It does not compare ordinary dropout with no dropout. Its qualitative loss-landscape comparison does not measure whether magnitude-aware sharpness tracks the train-test gap. None of V1–V8 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that layer-wise self-distillation between dropout-generated sub-models improves Transformer language-model performance across what they describe as 15 NLP datasets, without adding model parameters or changing the architecture. Their SST-2 analysis also reports flatter loss landscapes.
record.recipe_differences: Adds consistency losses between dropout-generated sub-models at hidden states, attention matrices, and output distributions; fine-tuning experiments use Transformer language models and NLP tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that varying training-set size changes performance; LR-Drop's reported advantage over BERT-base is 1% to 2% across the SST-2 subsets. Its loss-landscape analysis is limited to BERT-base on SST-2.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 5.4 reports qualitatively flatter loss landscapes for BERT-base trained with LR-Drop than with standard training on SST-2, using two random perturbation directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise consistency regularization between dropout-generated sub-models produces flatter loss landscapes in the tested BERT-base SST-2 setup.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation (2024)
record.problems: The loss-landscape result is qualitative and shown in a figure; no numerical flatness values or uncertainty are reported. The study does not measure the train-test gap in this analysis.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports numerous performance scores for LR-Drop and ablations in Tables 1–6, but these evaluate the paper's proposed method rather than an intervention named by the claim versions. They are therefore excluded under the row rules.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Adding ordinary dropout versus no dropout, training-set-size dependence of that effect, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay.
Whether magnitude-aware sharpness ranks train-test gaps among similarly fitted networks, including comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: The training-set-size experiments compare LR-Drop with baseline training and R-Drop; they do not isolate ordinary dropout's effect. The ablations remove consistency-loss terms, rather than dropout itself. The excluded performance tables therefore do not supply missing tests of V6.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Test error across widths beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and the stated tuning or recipe conditions.
Large versus small batch sizes and recipe adjustments.
The effect of adding ordinary dropout versus removing dropout, including the stated training-set-size and overfitting regimes.
Whether magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance tracks the train-test gap, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: BERT-base + LR-Drop
rows.operation_detail: Loss-landscape visualization around the empirical risk minimum under random perturbations in two directions.
rows.measure: Loss landscape flatness; authors state LR-Drop selects flatter landscapes than standard training.
rows.baseline: standard training; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: flatter loss landscape, as stated in text; numerical value figure only
rows.note: The text describes the figure's qualitative result. Perturbation directions are Gaussian with scale set to the variance of weight values; this is not the magnitude-aware perturbation measure in V7.
rows.check: The qualitative flatness finding is correctly attributed to Section 5.4 and Figure 2, but cannot establish any listed version's effect. No train-test gap, magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranking, or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures is reported. Retain as a finding outside the versions.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.4, Loss Landscape Analysis; Figure 2 caption identifies BERT-base, SST-2, standard training and LR-Drop.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Relies on dropout as a regularization tool without comparing ordinary dropout against no dropout. The landscape visualization does not test magnitude-aware sharpness against generalization gaps.
